title: The nuns return
hook: since the late twentieth century, full ordination for women has been renewed in several lineages; views on it differ

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ambedkar's vows, and a Buddhism built on equality. Your line: equal. Where did you catch yourself sorting people into higher and lower? Day one thousand seventeen.

Shaved heads, robes the color of turmeric, a line of women walking slowly into an ordination hall while monks wait inside to receive them. Scenes like this have happened in Sri Lanka, in Thailand, in the West, and each one has made news inside the Buddhist world. Why? Women have shaved their heads and kept precepts in Buddhist countries for a long time. But being a fully ordained nun, a bhikkhuni, is something else. In some lineages that order had disappeared, and nobody alive could pass it on. Today is about what happened when women went looking for a way back.
screen: `WOMEN WALK INTO THE HALL.` → `WHY IS THIS NEWS?` → `A LINE THAT HAD BROKEN.`

segments.voice: Start with the old story. In the Vinaya, the monastic rulebook, Mahapajapati, the woman who raised the Buddha, asks him to let women go forth. He hesitates. She and other women cut their hair, put on robes and follow him anyway, on foot, until their feet are swollen and dusty. Ananda speaks for them and asks the Buddha whether women can reach awakening. The Buddha says they can. So the order of nuns begins, with extra rules that place the nuns under the monks. Here's the difficulty. Full ordination is handed on by people who already have it, monks and nuns together. In the Theravada lands, the nuns' order died out or never took firm root, and in Tibet it seems never to have been brought in at all. Women kept practicing, as eight-precept or ten-precept nuns, but without full ordination. Then, in our own time, women from Sri Lanka, Thailand and elsewhere received full ordination, sometimes with help from Chinese and Korean nuns, whose line had continued. Views on this differ, and the people who hold them are sincere. Some Theravada monks and scholars say a broken line can't be restored from outside, so these ordinations don't count under the rules. Others say the Buddha himself opened the door to women, and the rules allow it to be opened again. Tibetan teachers have studied the question at length. Some nuns are glad to keep their present vows and want no change. It's a real argument about how to keep faith with rules handed down from teacher to student. And whatever any monastery decides, the women walking into those halls are taking the old story at its word.
screen: `MAHAPAJAPATI ASKS TO GO FORTH.` · `ORDINATION PASSES PERSON TO PERSON.` · `THE NUNS' LINE BREAKS, THEN RETURNS.` · `SINCERE VIEWS ON BOTH SIDES.` · then, large: `WOMEN CAN AWAKEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like it: honor a woman who ordained. Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind Mahapajapati on that long road, her feet sore, still walking. Or a nun you've read about or met, or a woman in any tradition who gave her life to practice when it wasn't easy. You don't need her name. Just hold the picture: someone who went forth. Let a little respect rise for her, the way you'd stand when someone walks into a room. When the mind wanders, come back to her steps. The bell holds the time.
The nuns return. The bhikkhuni ordination, lost in some lineages and renewed in some, while sincere teachers still differ about it. Today's words.
Your line: the nuns return. Today, find the name of one Buddhist nun, living or long ago, and read one thing she said. Day one thousand seventeen.

howItsDone: In some Theravada and Mahayana communities women now receive full bhikkhuni ordination from monks and nuns together; in others women live as eight- or ten-precept nuns, and the question of renewal is discussed openly and settled differently by different communities.

original.note: Pali bhikkhuni: a fully ordained Buddhist nun.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhist nuns are just women who shave their heads.
what it means: full ordination as a bhikkhuni is handed on person to person; where the line broke, some lineages have renewed it, and views differ.
what a scholar hears: a Vinaya question, whether ordination from an East Asian line can restore a Theravada or Tibetan order that lapsed.

sources.ref: Vinaya Pitaka, Cullavagga X (the going forth of Mahapajapati)

notes: Mahapajapati story paraphrased from Cullavagga X / AN 8.51: shaved heads, robes, swollen feet, Ananda's question, the Buddha's answer that women can attain the fruits. Confirm details and that 'extra rules placing nuns under monks' fairly summarizes the garudhammas.

Claim that the Theravada bhikkhuni order died out and that full ordination for women was never established in Tibet: confirm wording ('seems never to have been brought in'). No dates given on purpose.
Renewed ordinations (Sri Lanka, Thailand, the West) with help from Chinese/Korean (Dharmaguptaka) nuns: stated without dates or numbers; confirm.
Views presented without ranking: Theravada objection on lineage grounds, supporters' view, Tibetan study, nuns content with current vows. Keeper should check fairness.
Index word is the title head 'The nuns return'; kept exactly.
Editor pass: removed time spans not in the cited text ("in recent decades" -> "in our own time", "for centuries" -> "from teacher to student") and softened "still makes news" in the hook.
Audit pass: 'the nuns' order died out' across Theravada countries overgeneralized (it lapsed in Sri Lanka; in Thailand and Burma it arguably never took firm root); reworded.
